title: A closed theory of oceanic turbulent transport

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a transferable theory for how ocean turbulence and eddies move water, heat and dissolved substances at scales that circulation models cannot resolve directly. A closure translates the resolved ocean state into these unresolved transport rates. Here, it would predict both mixing across density surfaces, called diapycnal mixing, and transport by eddies as winds, tides and surface heating or cooling change, without recalibrating its constants to each new climate.

The intended theory would connect external forcing, ocean geometry and the evolving circulation to internal-wave generation, propagation, energy transfer and breaking, boundary mixing, and mesoscale and submesoscale eddy transport. It would operate within a dynamical circulation model supplied with bathymetry and specified initial and boundary conditions. A present-day map of mixing could help constrain or evaluate it, but the sought capability is to predict how transport changes when the conditions change.

significance.text: If validated across independent forcing regimes, this would be a fundamental advance from prescribing uncertain transport parameters toward predicting ocean transport from interacting physical processes. The observed overturning circulation depends on mechanical and buoyancy forcing acting together within geographic constraints. A successful closure would allow watermass transformation—the conversion of water between density classes—and the physical movement of heat and tracers to emerge more reliably from that coupled system.

The consequences could extend over centuries. The retained abstract of the 2017 abyssal-circulation paper connects understanding both the strength and structure of abyssal overturning with quantifying ocean heat and carbon storage on timescales longer than a century. More reliable transport predictions would therefore improve a central physical component of long-term storage estimates. This is a conditional consequence of achieving and validating the proposed closure, not a result already demonstrated by those sources.

The closure would not by itself determine total ocean heat uptake, carbon uptake or nutrient concentrations. Heat uptake also depends on air–sea exchange; carbon storage and nutrient supply require specified tracer sources and sinks and biogeochemical processes. Regional climate, ice sheets and ecosystems would still require their own coupled models. Its revolutionary value would lie in making the physical transport component predictive over a demonstrated range of conditions, rather than supplying a complete theory of every downstream response.

missing_breakthrough.text: The unresolved capability is a demonstrated closure that transfers across changes in wind, tidal and buoyancy forcing while retaining the same formulation and calibrated constants. Useful restricted theories and scalings already exist; their existence makes an absolute claim that there is no predictive law too strong. The broader challenge is to combine their domains into transport predictions that remain reliable when the forcing and resolved ocean state depart from the conditions used for calibration.

A historical symptom is the missing-mixing discrepancy. The 2025 review explains that classical scalings matched to observed thermocline depth and overturning require a diffusivity near 10⁻⁴ m² s⁻¹, whereas interior observations away from boundaries are around 10⁻⁵ m² s⁻¹. These numbers concern a particular scaling comparison and spatial setting. They do not establish that the whole ocean needs a uniform increase in diffusivity. The review attributes the discrepancy to multiple factors that require a fully three-dimensional account of circulation.

The concrete barriers include predicting where mechanical energy enters the ocean, how it travels between locations and scales, and where it produces irreversible mixing. Internal waves can travel far before breaking, so local forcing does not uniquely determine local dissipation. Boundary mixing, convection, overflows and eddy transport interact with stratification, topography and the large-scale flow. The 2025 review identifies poorly represented convection, overflows and internal mixing, together with uncertainty about the fate of eddy energy. Identifying these processes and their energy sources is necessary, but it does not yet specify their changing fluxes.

A further requirement is an explicit scope: which spatial and temporal scales, stratification states, topographies and forcing regimes the closure is intended to cover. Synthesis: a convincing solution would connect responsive energy pathways to transport while distinguishing the closure's own errors from errors in surface forcing, geometry, resolved dynamics and tracer budgets. That scope must be stated before broad predictive claims can be assessed.

current_state.text: The strongest contemporary assessment retained in the supplied review is Roquet and colleagues' review published on 15 August 2025. It documents limited understanding of the controls on the structure and intensity of the global overturning circulation and large disagreements among models, especially under changed wind, tidal and buoyancy forcing. It raises concerns about confidence in future circulation projections; those concerns are an assessment of predictive limitations, not evidence that every model prediction is false. The supplied record establishes neither an achieved transferable closure nor a formal impossibility result.

The 2025 review gives a differentiated account of ocean energetics: roughly 2–4 TW to maintain the general circulation, about 1 TW of tidal power supplying the open-ocean internal-wave field, about 0.3 TW of that tidal power dissipating below 1 km, and about 0.6 TW of wind power entering the mean geostrophic interior. These estimates refer to different budgets and stages of energy transfer. In particular, the 0.3 TW is part of the tidal pathway, so the figures must not be summed as independent inputs. They show why the modern problem is broader than finding a single missing power source. They do not establish that uncertainty bounds have narrowed quantitatively since 2004.

The supplied review reports complete retained HTML and PDF text for the 2025 article. The PDF extraction contains spacing and column-order defects, but the relevant power estimates and model-disagreement passages were readable and corroborated by the HTML. The DOI and PDF versions are versions of the same article, not independent corroborating studies. Figures were not visually inspected, so the conclusions here rely on the reviewed textual evidence.

The 2017 work by de Lavergne and colleagues provides a geometric constraint on abyssal circulation pathways. Its retained extended-data caption explicitly limits interpretation of normalized mixing scenarios to transport structure rather than magnitude, because the scenario amplitudes were normalized to a fixed peak upwelling. This is a useful constraint on where circulation can occur, but it does not establish an untuned prediction of transport strength. The supplied evidence includes the abstract and extended-data captions, not the main article text; the figures themselves were not inspected.

The research notes attribute to Munk and Wunsch's 1998 Abyssal recipes II an estimate of 2.1 TW needed to maintain the abyssal density distribution against 30 Sv of deep-water formation. They also attribute a poorly constrained mechanical-energy budget assessment to Wunsch and Ferrari in 2004. Neither source has a retained artifact in the supplied evidence review, so those historical statements remain unverified here. The 1998 full text was not opened in the research record. These access limitations do not establish that either attribution is false.

The research notes additionally cite a mixed-layer-closure result attributed to Uchida and colleagues and dated 28 February 2026, with abstract-level access. No artifact for that citation was retained for the supplied review, so its specific findings and the claimed recent closure revision cannot be established here. More generally, the supplied freshness record is empty: developments after the 2025 review through 1 November 2026 have not been assessed. The date of this record therefore does not establish that the 2025 diagnosis remains exhaustive.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: supply external forcing, basin geometry, bathymetry and specified initial and boundary conditions, then predict basin-scale watermass transformation, overturning strength and a specified passive-tracer inventory within predeclared observational uncertainty. Define the tracer's sources and sinks, comparison metrics, spatial and temporal averaging, and uncertainty treatment before evaluation. These are proposed operational criteria, not an established community standard.
completion_criteria.label: Predict watermass transformation, overturning and tracer inventory within observational uncertainty

completion_criteria.text: Proposed transferability test: predict an independently constrained forced response in a process experiment or past climate state whose fluxes were not used to fit the closure. Keep the closure formulation and calibrated constants fixed across tests, while allowing predicted fluxes and any prognostic variables to respond to the resolved state. Specify the tested scales, topographies and forcing regimes in advance. Success in a finite collection of cases would establish demonstrated breadth over those cases, not literal universality.
completion_criteria.label: Predict independently constrained forced responses with unchanged closure and constants

completion_criteria.text: Proposed process requirement: represent internal-wave generation, propagation, energy transfer and breaking, and connect the resulting energy dissipation to mixing without inserting today's dissipation geography as a fixed answer. Evaluate the associated boundary and eddy transports as part of the coupled calculation. A fit to the present ocean or a completed energy inventory whose transport fluxes remain tuned would not meet this proposed criterion. Solving the mathematical regularity problem for the Navier–Stokes equations is not a prerequisite for this operational demonstration.
completion_criteria.label: Connect internal-wave dynamics and dissipation to mixing with untuned transports

completion_criteria.text: Evaluation should examine more than a single maximum overturning transport. The 2025 review identifies ventilation age, deep western boundary-current strength, convection depth and watermass tracers as useful diagnostics. These provide a scientific basis for checking whether apparently successful bulk predictions also reproduce relevant circulation pathways and watermass histories.
completion_criteria.label: Reproduce circulation pathways and watermass histories beyond bulk overturning

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundary: release sufficient equations, parameter values, forcing specifications, numerical configuration and evaluation data for independent groups to repeat the tests. Report failures and sensitivity to observational and numerical uncertainty alongside successes. State the computational cost, resolution requirements and conditions outside the demonstrated domain so that practical usefulness can be judged separately from accuracy in selected experiments.
completion_criteria.label: Enable independent replication with reported uncertainties, failures and practical limits

related_concepts.text: Roster-based scope interpretation: OCE-07, The stability class of the global overturning circulation, is the closest conceptual neighbor. OCE-01 concerns transport laws that could enter a stability calculation; OCE-07 concerns how the circulation responds to disturbances and whether its present state is stable. A transferable closure would inform that calculation without itself determining the stability class. Only OCE-07's title is supplied, so this distinction does not establish its detailed requirements.

Roster-based scope interpretation: OCE-02, Synoptic sensing of the ocean interior, could provide observations for constraining and testing transport predictions. OCE-04, Persistent mobile operations at full ocean depth, and OCE-10, Basin-scale underwater positioning without surfacing, could enable sustained measurements along relevant pathways. Their central advances concern observing and operating in the ocean; OCE-01 concerns predicting unresolved physical transport.

Roster-based scope interpretation: OCE-03, A predictive closure of the biological carbon pump, and OCE-09, A predictive theory of pelagic size structure and trophic transfer, overlap through the movement of nutrients, organisms and carbon-bearing material. OCE-01 would supply physical transport to coupled models. Biological production, particle processing, organism size structure and trophic transfer require additional explanations, so success in physical transport would not complete either biological concept.

Roster-based scope interpretation: OCE-06, A verified law of ice-shelf basal melting, overlaps where ocean transport controls the delivery of heat to ice. A transport closure could improve the surrounding ocean calculation, while the melting law addresses the exchange and response at the ice–ocean interface. OCE-05, Closure of ocean–crust fluid and biogeochemical exchange, concerns another boundary exchange system; physical transport would help determine dispersal after exchange without alone specifying crustal fluid circulation or reactions.

Roster-based scope interpretation: OCE-08, Continuous centimeter-level geodesy of the seismogenic seafloor, has a more indirect relationship. Seafloor measurement capabilities may share infrastructure with ocean observations, but its target is precise deformation measurement rather than a turbulent transport law. The supplied titles do not establish a stronger dependency. All roster entries remain distinct.

change_log.reason: Makes the innovation understandable without implying that a closure alone predicts the complete ocean state.

change_log.reason: The reviewed evidence also describes useful restricted theories and scalings.

change_log.reason: Avoids double counting and the misleading interpretation of a single missing-power remainder.

unresolved_issues: The intended spatial and temporal scales, forcing regimes and acceptable computational cost of the proposed closure remain unspecified.
Observational uncertainty metrics, numerical tolerances, tracer budgets and independent validation cases have not been selected.
The Munk–Wunsch 2.1 TW and 30 Sv attribution and the Wunsch–Ferrari historical assessment require retained evidence for verification.
The identity, findings and publication details of the citation attributed to Uchida and colleagues require verification beyond the research notes' abstract-level account.
The 2017 main article text and figures were not assessed in the supplied review; the supported interpretation is limited to the retained abstract and captions.
Developments after the 2025 review through 1 November 2026 have not been assessed because the supplied freshness record is empty.
Related-concept definitions beyond their roster titles were not supplied, so the proposed overlap and scope distinctions remain editorial interpretations.

brief.title: Predicting ocean mixing as the climate changes
possible: Scientists could predict how the ocean moves heat and dissolved substances as winds, tides and surface heating change. The same theory would keep working without having its constants adjusted for each new climate.
It would calculate transport by turbulence and eddies—swirling currents—too small for circulation models to represent directly, including mixing between waters of different densities.
why: Climate researchers would gain more reliable predictions of the physical movement that carries heat and carbon through the ocean. This would improve a central part of estimates of how the ocean stores them over centuries.

sources.showed: Their review brought together how mixing, sinking water, winds and geography shape global ocean circulation. Models still disagree about its response to changing conditions.
sources.quote: Clearly, the GOC as we observe it depends on both mechanical and buoyancy forcings acting together.
sources.cited_for: Ocean circulation depends on interacting processes that a predictive transport theory must connect.
sources.not_established: The review does not demonstrate a transport theory that works across changed conditions without adjusting its constants.

sources.showed: A later version of the same work.
This is a study of the energy needed to maintain the deep ocean's density distribution through mixing.
sources.cited_for: It addresses the energy requirements of deep ocean mixing.
sources.not_established: An energy requirement alone does not predict where mixing occurs or how transport changes.

sources.showed: This is an assessment of the ocean's mechanical energy budget and its uncertainties.
sources.cited_for: It addresses uncertainty about the energy supporting ocean circulation.
sources.not_established: An energy budget alone does not establish transport predictions across changing conditions.

sources.showed: They showed that seafloor shape constrains the routes taken by deep ocean water. Their mixing comparisons addressed circulation structure rather than its strength.
sources.quote: the depth distribution of the seafloor compels dense southern-origin waters to flow northward below a depth of about 4 kilometres
sources.cited_for: Seafloor geometry constrains deep circulation pathways.
sources.not_established: Constraints on pathways do not establish predictions of transport strength without adjusted constants.

sources.showed: This is work on representing unresolved transport in the ocean's mixed surface layer.
sources.cited_for: It concerns a restricted part of the broader transport problem.
sources.not_established: A surface-layer theory alone would not establish predictive transport throughout the ocean.

shown: Useful theories already predict transport under restricted conditions. De Lavergne and colleagues showed how seafloor geometry constrains deep circulation routes. Roquet and colleagues explain how the main controls interact, but no theory has demonstrated the full capability.
missing: No combined theory has demonstrated reliable transport predictions across changed winds, tides and surface heating without adjusting its constants.
Energy pathways must predict where mixing occurs, including energy carried far from its source by waves inside the ocean.
The theory must calculate transport near boundaries and by eddies as part of the changing circulation.
Physical transport alone cannot determine total heat or carbon uptake; surface exchanges and biological and chemical processes also matter.

milestones.label: Basin predictions agree with observations
milestones.explanation: Predictions must match observed changes between water density classes, sinking and rising circulation, and the amount of a substance carried by the flow, within agreed uncertainty. This tests basin-scale accuracy.

milestones.label: Predictions transfer without adjusting constants
milestones.explanation: The same theory and constants must predict independently measured responses to changed conditions outside those used to fit it. This tests whether its success carries beyond familiar conditions.

milestones.label: Wave energy predicts mixing and transport
milestones.explanation: The theory must connect the creation, travel and breaking of waves inside the ocean to mixing, alongside boundary and eddy transport, without tuning the resulting flows. This connects energy pathways to transport.

milestones.label: Circulation routes and water histories also agree
milestones.explanation: Tests must reproduce current pathways, how deep water sinks and how long water has been away from the surface. These checks reveal errors that an accurate total circulation rate could hide.

milestones.label: Independent groups reproduce results and establish practical limits
milestones.explanation: Other groups must be able to repeat the tests using shared equations, settings and data, with uncertainties, failures and computing needs reported. This establishes reproducibility and practical usefulness.

uncertain: The range of ocean conditions, distances and times the theory should cover remains undefined.
Acceptable errors, independent test cases and computational costs still need to be agreed.
Success across selected cases would establish a tested range of usefulness, rather than validity under every possible condition.

page.title: Ocean turbulence and eddy transport closure
page.definition: A closure calculates transport by motions too small for a circulation model to resolve. One coupled formulation predicts mixing across density surfaces and transport by eddies, or swirling currents, as winds, tides and surface heat and freshwater fluxes change, keeping its calibrated constants fixed.

goal.need: Southern Ocean overturning, the circulation connecting surface and deep waters, combines opposing wind-driven and eddy-induced transports of comparable magnitude. Deep and bottom waters are renewed from the surface over decades to millennia, redistributing heat and carbon. Predicting that circulation requires representing both eddy transport and mixing across density surfaces.

figures.caption: Southern Ocean overturning estimates in the 2025 review
figures.note: Estimates correspond to zonal-mean wind stress of 0.1–0.15 N m⁻². One sverdrup (Sv) is 10⁶ m³ s⁻¹.

completion.title: An unchanged coupled closure predicts ocean transport across independent forcing regimes.
completion.criterion: In a global circulation model, one coupled closure predicts mixing across density surfaces and eddy transport under independently constrained changes in each of wind, tidal and surface heat/freshwater forcing. Its formulation and calibrated constants remain fixed. Mixing rates, overturning and heat or passive-tracer transport agree with independent observations or process-resolving simulations within their quantified comparison uncertainties. Geometry, initial and boundary conditions, resolution, averaging and the tested forcing range are specified.
completion.set_by: Atlas operational criterion, inferred from published programme goals and closure-generalization studies.
completion.basis: Searched SCOR ocean-mixing recommendations, NSF CPT solicitations, CLIVAR/COMMODORE workshop objectives, TRR 181 goals and published closure benchmarks for a joint completion test. No prescribed forcing suite or joint acceptance threshold was found. The proposed test combines computed mixing, global-model verification and the developers' goal of transfer without retuning over a stated domain.

milestones.title: A closure predicts laboratory mixing within experimental uncertainty.
milestones.criterion: Given the forcing and geometry, predict irreversible mixing in a controlled experiment with a stable density gradient, withheld from calibration, within quantified experimental uncertainty. Dossmann and colleagues, published on 25 August 2016, reported 27 experiments with a 5 cm ridge and 10 with a 16 cm ridge, spanning three flow regimes. Their measurements distinguish mixing close to topography from mixing associated with radiated internal waves.
milestones.set_by: Atlas operational criterion. Searches of SCOR recommendations and laboratory mixing studies found no common laboratory acceptance threshold.

milestones.title: A coupled ocean closure exchanges energy with zero spurious sources or sinks.
milestones.criterion: The closure's energy-transfer terms between resolved flow, eddies, internal waves and turbulence cancel in the summed energy budget. External fluxes and conversion to heat account for its energy change. Eden, Czeschel and Olbers coupled these reservoirs in three approximately consistent quasi-global model versions in 2014. Their implemented model retained overall energy-budget residuals up to several percent.
milestones.set_by: Energetic-consistency convention in ocean modelling, stated explicitly by Eden, Czeschel and Olbers in their 2014 paper's summed energy budget.
milestones.threshold_quote: the energy related to the mean variables would interact with all parameterized forms of energy without any spurious energy sources or sinks.

milestones.title: An ocean closure measurably improves a global circulation simulation.
milestones.criterion: Implement a transport parameterization in a global circulation model and verify measurable improvement in its target process. The NSF programme supplies no common numerical error cutoff. On 21 June 2024, Brüggemann and colleagues reported internal-wave-driven mixing in MITgcm, FESOM and ICON-O. All three improved agreement with observationally inferred mixing patterns and energetics. Their deep overturning responses differed.
milestones.set_by: NSF Climate Process and Modeling Teams programme, solicitation NSF 09-568, objectives and implementation requirements in Section II.
milestones.threshold_quote: Implement and verify improved parameterizations for a few processes that have a mature observational and theoretical base.

milestones.title: One coupled closure matches present-day mixing and circulation within observational uncertainty.
milestones.criterion: At a specified resolution and averaging period, the coupled mixing and eddy closures reproduce independent present-day mixing rates, overturning and temperature/salinity distributions within quantified observational comparison uncertainties, using one parameter set. On 20 February 2026, Uchida and colleagues compared two mixed-layer eddy schemes in three global ocean simulations and found ventilation sensitive to their interaction with surface boundary-layer mixing.
milestones.set_by: Atlas operational criterion. Searches of NSF, CLIVAR and TRR 181 targets and global-model comparisons found no joint present-day acceptance threshold.

results.finding: In one ECCOv4r4 reconstruction, the eddy parameterization produces an 860 GW potential-energy sink.
results.detail: The sink is not transferred to eddy kinetic energy. The analysis does not demonstrate a coupled closure with cancelling transfers among all four reservoirs.
